name: Open Spinal Dysraphism

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Radiological Diagnostic Criteria for Open Spinal Dysraphism

criteria.description: Presence of an exposed spinal cord or meninges protruding through a vertebral defect
Identification of vertebral and spinal cord malformation on prenatal or postnatal imaging (ultrasound, MRI)
Neurological impairment consistent with spinal cord involvement such as lower limb weakness or bladder dysfunction
Elevated maternal serum or amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein levels during pregnancy

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of visible spinal sac with exposed neural tissue plus confirmatory imaging findings
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Prenatal diagnosis is often possible via ultrasound and maternal serum screening.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Exposed spinal cord with meningeal sac protrusion
pathognomonic.notes: Visible at birth as a sac-like protrusion on the back
searchTerms: open spinal cord with covering sac

pathognomonic.notes: Manifested as urinary incontinence or retention
searchTerms: bladder control issues from nerve damage

common.notes: Often associated with Arnold-Chiari II malformation

common.symptomName: Sensory loss below the lesion level
searchTerms: loss of feeling below affected area
brain tissue herniation at skull base

occasional.notes: Progressive neurological deterioration due to spinal cord tethering
May be secondary to hydrocephalus or other CNS anomalies

laboratory: Elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein during pregnancy
imaging: Prenatal ultrasound showing spinal defect and meningeal sac
MRI demonstrating open spinal cord defect and associated anomalies
genetic: No single gene mutation identified; multifactorial etiology with genetic and environmental factors
other: Physical examination revealing exposed neural tissue at birth
Neurological assessment showing motor and sensory deficits

distinguishingFeatures: Skin-covered spinal defect without exposed neural tissue
Small vertebral defect without neural tissue involvement
No visible sac or neurological deficits

redFlags: Visible spinal sac with exposed neural tissue at birth
Progressive lower limb weakness or paralysis
Signs of increased intracranial pressure indicating hydrocephalus
references: Wong S, et al. Open Spinal Dysraphism: Clinical Features and Management. Neurology Clinics. 2023.
Orphanet: Open Spinal Dysraphism. Orphanet Report Series. 2024.
Pang D. Spinal Dysraphism: A Review. Neurosurgery. 2022.
